passage: Monday was allowance day, and at the school's savings-club table Irfan sir was already counting envelopes. Yamini took her 400 rupees from her bag, counted out a fifth, 80 rupees, and slid it into her envelope marked TRIP. Irfan sir wrote her name in the register. “Before the canteen?” he asked. “Before anything,” Yamini said. “If I wait for leftovers, there aren't any.” Last month she had promised herself she would save whatever remained on Friday, and found only coins. She tucked the rest into her wallet and walked to the canteen with 320 in her hand, and it felt like plenty.

qa.q: How much did Yamini put into her envelope?
qa.a: Yamini counted out a fifth, 80 rupees, and slid it into her envelope.

qa.q: What does Yamini's remark about leftovers suggest she felt after last month?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated with herself, since she had promised to save what remained and found only coins.

qa.q: What could Yamini do if the fixed amount feels too tight some weeks?
qa.a: She could lower the fixed portion a little but still set it aside first, since saving first keeps the habit steady.

qa.q: How might Irfan sir see Yamini's choice?
qa.a: Irfan sir may feel pleased to see a student set money aside before spending, since he asked about the canteen and wrote her name in the register.

grounding: On the day the allowance arrives, a student sets aside a fixed portion before spending, so saving does not depend on leftovers.

passage:
Dear Pradeep Anna,
You asked how I finally saved for the cricket bat when I never could before. It's the trick you told me about, and it actually worked.
Before, I used to spend first and save whatever was left at the end of the month. There was never anything left. Not once.
So in January I changed the order. Appa gives me my allowance on the first Sunday of the month. That same afternoon, before I even go to the shop, I put a fixed part of it into a brown envelope marked BAT and hand the envelope to Amma to keep in her cupboard. Only then do I spend the rest.
The first month it felt like I had less money. By the third month I didn't notice. By May the envelope had enough, and Appa took me to the sports shop.
I'm keeping the envelope. Now it says BOOKS.
Karthik

qa.q: Where does the envelope marked BAT go?
qa.a: To Amma, to keep in her cupboard.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel about the new order at first, and later?
qa.a: Karthik felt short of money at first, but by the third month didn't notice, and felt proud when the bat was bought.

qa.q: What else could Karthik consider as the savings grow?
qa.a: Asking Appa or Amma whether a savings account would be a better place than an envelope.

qa.q: How might Pradeep Anna feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Pradeep Anna would likely feel pleased the advice worked and proud of a younger cousin who stuck with it.

grounding: Shows a student putting a fixed part of the allowance into a separate envelope on the day it arrives, before spending, so saving doesn't depend on leftovers.

passage:
Ujjwal, you asked how I saved enough for the school trip to Rishikesh. I'm Vandana, and I'll tell you, because it's embarrassingly simple.
For a whole year I tried to save what was left over. You know how that goes. Nothing's ever left over. There's always a samosa, a pen, a recharge.
Then Papa helped me open a small student savings account at the bank near our school. And we made a deal: on the day my pocket money arrives, the first thing I do, before anything else, is put a fixed part into that account. At first I did it at the bank counter; now Papa helps me do it on his phone the same evening.
The rest is mine to spend, no guilt. If it runs out on the twentieth, it runs out.
It took me eight months. But in the end I didn't have to ask anyone for the trip money. That felt amazing, honestly.

qa.q: How long did it take Vandana to save for the trip?
How did Vandana feel about not having to ask for the trip money?
qa.a: Vandana felt proud and happy, saying it honestly felt amazing.

qa.q: What else could help Vandana if an unexpected cost comes up mid-month?
qa.a: Talking to Papa about it rather than quietly dipping into the trip savings, so the plan stays clear.

qa.q: What might Ujjwal take from hearing this?
qa.a: Ujjwal may be surprised that it's so simple and tempted to try saving first instead of saving leftovers.

grounding: Shows a student moving a fixed part of pocket money into a savings account on the day it arrives, before spending, so saving doesn't rely on leftovers.
